units: a thick wool jacket soaks up water in a downpour
the wet cloth drags at the shoulders and warps the sleeves
the lining holds the damp all evening
workshops spread hot wax over the outer face
the wax fills the tiny gaps without stopping the fiber from breathing
a thin membrane can be set between the wool and the lining
that film pushes vapor off the back and turns the drops away
the treated garment stays supple and keeps its cut
brushing and a fresh coat of wax extend the protection
text: Rain hits a thick wool jacket and the wool drinks it in. Within minutes the wet cloth drags heavily at the shoulders, the sleeves lose their shape and hang crooked, and the lining holds that damp all through the evening. Workshops looked for an answer that would leave the fiber alone. The first one is a hot wax, spread thin across the outer face, which fills the tiny gaps without stopping the wool from breathing. Water rolls off, and the jacket still lets air through. The second is a thin membrane, slipped between the wool and the lining. That film pushes the vapor off a warm back outward and turns the drops away. Either way the coat stays supple and keeps the line it was cut to. Brush the surface, lay down a fresh coat of wax, and the protection holds through a whole season.

units: the speaker finds the choice between natural fiber and made fiber a badly framed question
fine wool warms without any weight
wool takes up sweat and releases it with no smell
wool pills as soon as a bag strap rubs it
made fiber dries fast and shrugs off abrasion
made fiber sticks to the skin as soon as you push yourself
a loose knit forgives a heavy meal and takes another layer
a tight top draws the figure and wants the exact size
the speaker keeps both and decides by use
text: People keep asking me whether they ought to buy natural knitwear or a made fiber, and to my mind the question is badly framed from the start. The two families were never promising the same thing. Fine wool warms you with no weight at all, takes up the sweat off your back and lets it go without a smell, then pills the moment a bag strap rubs across it. A made fiber dries in an hour and shrugs off abrasion, holds its shape wash after wash, but sticks to your skin the second you push yourself. Look at the cut as well, because comfort really lives right there. A loose knit forgives a heavy meal and takes another layer underneath. A tight top draws the figure and wants the exact size, nothing near it. So I keep both of them on the shelf and decide by what the day ahead asks of me.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the dyer works in a workshop with a low ceiling
she sorts her skeins before dipping them
she knows the fibers by touch
she boils her baths out of bark and root
her baths give a deep blue or a shifting red
she writes every proportion into a notebook
without those notes a good bath could never be made again
her clients bring her tired woolens and speckled jackets
those clients refuse to throw their clothes away
text: The dyer works under a low ceiling, and she sorts her skeins on a bench before anything at all goes into the vat. She sums her whole trade up in three habits, without making much of any of them. First the material: her fingers tell a silky strand from a coarse tuft, and she needs no label at all to do it. Then the color. She boils her baths out of bark and root, and what comes up is a deep blue, or a red that shifts as the light moves over it. Third, memory. Every single proportion goes into a stained notebook, because a bath that turns out well will not turn out twice on luck alone. Her clients hand her tired woolens, dulled scarves, jackets gone speckled that they will not throw away. She promises little, gives back honest color, and her notebook is worth far more than her vat.

units: the narrator finds a quilted coat on a modest rack
at first he takes it for graceless
the weeks that follow argue with that first judgment
the quilting holds a layer of warm air in the rain
the high collar closes the throat against the wind without gripping it
the cloth creased by so many journeys takes on a living look
by the end of winter the coat lightens as the layers come off
the narrator concludes that a garment is judged by wear and not on display
text: I found the quilted coat on a modest rack one evening, and I wrote it off at once as graceless, too thick, too careful, sewn for people who take no chances. The weeks that followed argued with me. Under thin rain the quilting held a layer of warm air that nothing scattered, and my shoulders stayed dry the whole way home. When the wind began working through the narrow streets, the high collar showed its sense: it closed my throat against the cold without gripping it. Then came the squalls, and the cloth, creased by so many journeys, took on a living look that fresh cloth never shows. By the end of winter, stripped of the layers it had sheltered, it hung straight and light again. So I will say it plainly. A coat is not judged on a hanger. It is judged after a season of rain and walking.

units: the reader washed a sweater that shrank
a wool fiber is covered in tiny scales
heat lifts those scales up
the tumbling of the drum tangles the fibers together
tangled fibers cannot go back where they started
the shrinking is therefore beyond repair
wash in cold water with no violent spin
dry the piece flat on a towel
a rinse with a little vinegar softens the knit
text: Dear neighbor, you asked me what had happened to your favorite sweater, and the answer turns out to be purely mechanical. A wool fiber is not smooth. It carries tiny scales, laid over one another the way roof tiles are laid. Hot water lifts those scales up. The drum then shoves the fibers against each other, and the raised scales catch and lock like little hooks. The knit closes in on itself, the surface goes hard, and the sweater drops a whole size. No amount of ironing will pull it open again, because nothing can unhook what the tumbling wound together. With the next piece, use cold water and a gentle spin, then lay it flat on a thick towel to dry. A last rinse with a little vinegar softens the knit and gives it back the drape it had. Take good care of yourself, and write soon.

units: the question is whether fine knits should be given up because they pill
pilling starts with short fibers working their way to the surface
friction rolls those fibers into little balls
a long twisted yarn cuts the fault down sharply
the piece must be turned inside out before washing
loads carrying rough materials should be avoided
a fabric shaver lifts the balls off without gouging the knit
the sweater must be folded flat and never hung
a garment handled this way lasts through long seasons
text: Should fine knitwear be given up on the grounds that it pills? The answer calls for a distinction. The fault starts with short fibers that work their way to the surface, where friction rolls them into tight little balls. A long, firmly twisted yarn cuts the trouble down sharply, and the composition label tells you more about that than the look of the piece or the price shown in the window. What can be done with a garment already marked? Turn it inside out before washing, keep it clear of loads that carry rough materials, and run a fabric shaver over it, which lifts the balls off without gouging the knit. Should storage change too? It should. A fitted sweater sags at the shoulders on a hanger, so fold it flat. Handled that way, a fine woolen goes through long seasons unspoiled.

units: a customer cannot decide between two jackets
the close cut flatters him but catches his arm when he reaches
the wider cut gives him back his reach
he is afraid the wider cut will make him look sloppy
the saleswoman tells him to think about what he will use it for
the close jacket suits meetings and meals taken sitting down
the wide jacket suits walking about and carrying bags
she offers to take in the shoulders of the wide jacket
the customer leaves with the wide jacket after that offer
text: The customer stood a long while between two jackets hanging on the same rail, and he laid his trouble out plainly. The close cut flattered him, he said, but it caught his arm the second he reached toward a high shelf. The wider cut gave him back his reach, though he was afraid it would leave him looking sloppy. The saleswoman heard him out patiently, then set the two side by side for him. The first jacket, she said, serves meetings and meals taken sitting down, where nobody moves much and the outline counts. The second one goes with walking about, standing around, a bag hanging off one shoulder. She added that taking in the shoulders would tighten the second one without costing it any ease. He thought about it for a while, then left with the wider jacket and the alteration booked.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the earliest cloth comes from stalks soaked in water
those stalks give a cool fiber that creases at the smallest movement
taming herds brought a warm springy fiber
that fiber is spun by hands trained from childhood
a shiny thread is unwound off cocoons
the shiny thread travels down very long roads
a downy seed capsule yields a washable cheap cloth
better looms later turn out a ribbed velvet
every new material redrew the ordinary wardrobe
text: Have you ever wondered where our cloth actually comes from? Let us take it one family at a time, with no hurry about it at all. The oldest of them all starts with stalks soaked in water, then beaten and combed out: what comes off is a cool fiber, easy to wear once the heat sets in, and creased by the smallest movement. Next comes the fleece of tamed herds, warm and springy, spun at home by hands trained from childhood. Later a shiny thread turns up, unwound off cocoons, light enough to carry down endless roads and dear enough to be kept for finery. Then a downy seed capsule yields a washable cloth, cheap enough to clothe whole populations at once. Better looms add ribbed velvet on top of that, thick and striped. Every one of these materials went on to redraw the ordinary wardrobe.

units: the fleece comes off the animal in a single piece
a wash carries off the grease and the dust
carding pulls the tangles apart and lays the fibers in one direction
twist turns the ribbon of fibers into a yarn that holds
the yarn is then stretched on a loom to make cloth
dyeing can happen on the yarn or on the finished cloth
fulling in water draws the cloth tighter and denser
cutting and stitching finish the making of the garment
text: It all starts in a shed at the far end of a field, when the shearer works the fleece off in a single piece. That greasy mass goes straight into water: it is washed, the dust and the twigs are picked out, and it is spread to dry. Then comes carding, which pulls the tangles apart and lays every strand in one direction. The ribbon coming off the combs goes to the wheel or the machine, where twist turns it into a yarn that holds. That yarn is stretched on a loom, crossed patiently with a second one, and even cloth grows steadily under the weaver's hands. Dye can go on at this point, or earlier, on the bare yarn. Fulling in warm water then draws the fibers closer, leaving a denser surface and a softer hand. Cutting and stitching finish off the road that leads from animal to worn coat.

units: the night watchman wears a coat worn through
he lends that coat to an apprentice who is shivering
she finds a lining sewn by hand
the lining carries embroidered initials and a hidden pocket
the pocket holds a square of shiny cloth
the watchman explains that the square came off a dress his mother wore
the apprentice takes the coat to a seamstress to be mended
the watchman accepts the mending but refuses an unworn coat
text: The night watchman's coat was worn through at the elbows, and that had never troubled the man who owned it. An apprentice stood shivering outside the empty warehouse, hands pushed under her arms, and he held the coat out to her without a word of explanation. Pulling it closed, she felt a lining sewn by hand, initials embroidered in dark thread, a pocket tucked away under the seam. Inside it lay a square of silky cloth, bright, smooth against her frozen fingers as still water. He said at last that the square had come off a dress his mother used to wear, and that he kept it there to have it on him. The apprentice carried the coat to a seamstress, who rebuilt the elbows and strengthened the sleeves. He took the mending without a fuss. The unworn coat he was offered afterward he refused flatly.
